CHICAGO, IL: A federal judge in the Central District of Illinois ruled Friday that Illinois is not required to share sensitive registered voter data with the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), finding that the government’s broad demand for Illinois’ voters confidential information runs afoul of federal law.


This decision marks the 19th consecutive federal court ruling nationwide rejecting the DOJ’s attempts to capture unredacted state voter rolls.


The ruling stems from a December 2025 lawsuit— *United States v. Matthews* —filed after the Illinois State Board of Elections refused to turn over its unredacted voter registration file, a file that contains sensitive personal data about millions of Illinois residents including each individual’s full name, date of birth, address, driver’s license number and partial Social Security number. Shortly after the lawsuit was filed, Common Cause, the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, and three Illinois voters—Pablo Mendoza, Brian Beals, and Alejandra Ibañez—moved to intervene in the case, a motion that was granted.


These clients are represented by Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, the ACLU National Voting Rights Project and the ACLU of Illinois.


“This ruling is another decisive rejection of the federal government’s attempts to bypass its limits of power,” said **Ethan Herenstein, staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project.** “The Trump administration cannot manufacture a voter fraud crisis to justify a sweeping up of sensitive personal information from millions of Americans.”


“This victory makes it 19-0 in stopping the federal government from seizing your private voter data,” **said Maryam Jazini Dorcheh, Vice President of Litigation at Common Cause.** “The record is clear: states run elections —not the president. We won’t stop fighting to protect voters’ privacy.”


“The entire premise for this lawsuit is the myth of massive noncitizen voter fraud — a canard that has been repeatedly debunked even by supporters of this administration,” said **Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights (ICIRR)** . “We are pleased that the court saw through this ruse and dismissed the case.”


“Today’s ruling is a critical victory for the privacy rights of every Illinois voter,” said **Ami Gandhi, Director of the Midwest Voting Rights Program with Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights** . “The federal government’s attempt to seize sensitive personal records was an unprecedented overreach designed to intimidate voters and fuel false narratives about our election systems. By rejecting this demand, the court has sent a clear message that our democratic process will not be weaponized to harass or suppress Illinois voters, particularly naturalized citizens and people returning home from incarceration who are disproportionately targeted by these efforts.”


“We are grateful to the Court for rejecting the Trump Administration’s efforts to meddle in our State’s elections and create a nationwide database that can be used to harass voters,” added **Kevin Fee, Legal Director at the ACLU of Illinois.** “We must continue to fight the Administration’s lies about supposed voter fraud, and its attempt to suppress voting by sowing doubt and confusion about our elections. This case is one part of that fight.”


Read the court’s order dismissing the DOJ lawsuit here: https://www.aclu-il.org/app/uploads/2026/07/US-v.-Matthews-Order.pdf

### United States v. Matthews


The Department of Justice sued the Illinois Board of Elections, demanding the state produce its full, unredacted voter file, which contains highly sensitive and personal data on every voter in the state. This suit appears to be part of the federal government’s efforts to build a national voter database without congressional authorization and to improperly question the validity of state voter rolls.

### Voters Support Freedom and Democracy in Major Night for Civil Rights and Liberties


WASHINGTON – Following race projection announcements in key campaigns and in races that will determine the control of Congress, the American Civil Liberties Union released the following statement from Chief Political and Advocacy Officer Deirdre Schifeling on the results so far of the 2026 midterm elections: “Tonight, voters sent a clear message to politicians: You work for us. Since the day President Trump took office, his administration and allies have been working overtime to take away voters’ power. But American voters have shown through historic turnout that they’ve had enough of a rigged system designed to work for the people in power instead of for them. “From key state supreme court races in Michigan and North Carolina to state legislative races in Georgia and North Carolina, voters uniformly rejected candidates who threaten abortion rights and our right to vote. Voters also stood up for reproductive freedom in Missouri and Virginia, and permanently secured voting rights and marriage equality in Virginia. “However, our work is only half done, and now a new chapter begins. With a new Congress in Washington and state legislative sessions starting in January, now is our moment to create the representative, accountable democracy we have always deserved and remedy the failures of our system that led us to this point. We must unrig the system and ensure that government is used to make ordinary people’s lives better, not to enrich and entrench those in power.” As part of the ACLU’s “Firewall for Freedom” strategy, the organization and its PAC, ACLU Voter Education Fund, made their largest-ever commitment in down ballot races, spending $25.5 million across underfunded but critical state-level campaigns with an outsized impact on our rights and freedoms, from key ballot initiatives to state Supreme Court races, secretaries of state races, and state legislative races.

### Comments of the ACLU on "Decennial Census of the Population of Americans" (Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions)


The Census Bureau has proposed rules for the 2030 Census that would remove millions of noncitizens from the population count used to divide congressional seats among the states. This includes many noncitizens living in the United States lawfully. The rules would also change where everyone else is counted and bar the census from asking about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. The Constitution requires counting the “whole number of persons in each State,” and every census since 1790 has counted people where they live, regardless of citizenship. The proposal would distort political representation, weaken the count’s accuracy, and eliminate data needed to enforce the Voting Rights Act and other civil rights laws. The ALCU is urging the Bureau to withdraw the rule entirely.

### Voting Rights Groups Win Case to Protect Alaska’s Election Certification


Anchorage, AK – The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Alaska, Common Cause, and League of Women Voters of Alaska issued statements today after a federal judge rejected the Department of Justice’s last-minute attempt to block Alaska’s Senate election results if the Republican candidate did not win. “This desperate attempt to disenfranchise Alaska voters has been swiftly thrown out of court, and that is a win for democracy,” said Ari Savitzky, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project. “The court’s get-out-and-don’t-come-back ruling makes clear that preemptively blocking election results and running an inquisition into the sincerity of voters’ choices would be flatly illegal. Every American should be alarmed that their own Justice Department tried to put voters on trial for how they might vote. That should never happen in this country. The rule of law held, and voters should go to the polls with their heads held high. Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of Alaska, and individual Alaska voters, represented by the ACLU National Voting Rights Project and the ACLU of Alaska, intervened to protect the voting rights of Alaskans. The ruling rejects DOJ’s lawsuit because the relief the federal government sought was illegal and would have disrupted Alaska’s elections on the eve of voting and violated Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot. “This ruling is a victory for the people of Alaska, reaffirming their voices will be heard, and their votes will be counted,” said Virginia Kase Solomon, president and CEO of Common Cause. “The Trump administration keeps trying tricks to interfere in our election, but they keep failing because our democracy and people-power is strong. Common Cause will continue to defend Americans’ freedom to vote in free and fair elections because politicians don’t dictate election outcomes, people do.” “Today the court upheld our most fundamental voting rights by dismissing the federal government’s frivolous lawsuit,” said Lu-Anne Haukaas Lopez, Executive Director for the ACLU of Alaska. “The decision affirmed what we already know: Alaskans – not the president- decide our elections. The ACLU of Alaska is watching this election closely for other attempts to undermine our elections. We remain committed to protecting and defending the voting rights of all Alaskans.” “We are grateful the district court defended democracy today by dismissing this groundless, frivolous lawsuit,” said Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters. “The voters of Alaska have the right to decide who represents them in the United States Senate, and the Department of Justice has no right to interfere through its groundless demands.” Counting every vote takes time, and it’s unlikely that Alaskans will have final results on Election Night. Alaska election officials follow strict state laws that include steps for receiving, checking, processing, counting, reviewing, and certifying ballots. Some ballots, including mail ballots or ballots that require verification, may take longer to count. Election officials are required by law to certify the election results.


**Court Case:** United States v. Alaska
